description: As human curiosity grows, so does the will to explore, learn, and expand further into the universe. Because actions shape dreams into reality, our next great step is returning to the Moon—and finding the safest place to land. That is exactly what we are here to figure out. Whether you are a mission planner, a student, or simply passionate about space exploration, step inside and navigate the lunar south pole with us.
summary:
We developed a Lunar Landing Site Navigator application that allows users to select from all known lunar landing positions or add custom lunar coordinates at different dates to provide easy-to-interpret visuals and direct data on variations in solar power generation and direct-to-Earth communication at the landing position over time, while also considering surrounding terrain effects (terrain angles) and assuming the use of auto-rotating solar panels (to maximise solar power generation). 

This application allows us to find suitable landing locations and assess landing dates across the Moon’s surface, reducing mission planning time and aiding possible future landings. It also clarifies the difficulties faced in choosing landing positions - especially at the lunar south pole - such as the lack of sunlight, short direct-to-Earth communication windows, and uneven terrain causing extreme shadows to spread across the landing area. 

This may help us better understand conditions on the Moon and better face these challenges in the future. Additionally, it may boost the frequency of Moon landings - hopefully amplifying our collection of lunar data and knowledge - leading to improved insights into the history of the Moon and perhaps some hints about the universe’s secrets in the years to come.
details:
The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web dashboard that helps mission planners, educators, and space enthusiasts compare potential lunar landing sites across different dates. The dashboard does real-time geometric and topographic double-checks by comparing angles against local lunar terrain elevation profiles:

  • Direct-to-Earth Communications Check: The app compares the Earth-to-site elevation angle against surrounding lunar terrain horizon angles. When Earth clears the local terrain (specifically accounting for a 2.00° clearance angle above the terrain horizon to establish a 100% link), a direct line-of-sight communication window is marked as ACTIVE/ONLINE. Communication signal strength is modeled proportionally to the percentage of the visible Earth disc, assuming uniform signal distribution across the visible surface.
  • Solar Power Generation Check: The app compares the Sun-to-site elevation angle against local terrain ridge angles. Whenever the Sun rises above surrounding ridges, incident sunlight reaches the landing site. Solar power potential is calculated proportionally to the visible percentage of a uniformly bright solar disc, assuming the lander utilizes auto-rotating (Sun-tracking) solar arrays to maximize energy capture.

Dashboard Features

  • Quick-scan calendar: Displays two dots beneath each data so users can spot good days when both power and communications are active.
  • Monthly overview graph: Plots continuous power and communication percentages as two trend lines, allowing planner to visually see the window where the 100% power and communications overlap.
  • Event Countdowns: Displays real-time countdown timers to the next sunrise/sunset (power status change) and Earth-rise/Earth-set (communication status change). 

By lowering the barrier to evaluating lunar surface conditions, the Lunar Landing Site Navigator can streamline early-stage mission planning and improve agility when launch dates or target coordinates shift. 

Potential Future Enhancements

  • Lunar Dust & Regolith Levitation: Consider factor of atmospheric or surface dust accumulation on solar arrays that could degrade power efficiency.
  • Space Weather & Solar Storms: Electromagnetic interference and radiation events that could disrupt direct-to-Earth communications.
